content: The systematic review and meta-analysis conducted by Lam et al. evaluated the efficacy and safety of naltrexone in treating amphetamine and methamphetamine use disorders. This study synthesized data from randomized controlled trials to provide evidence-based insights into the potential benefits and risks of naltrexone for individuals with these substance use disorders. Minozzi et al. reviewed psychosocial interventions for individuals misusing psychostimulants. Their Cochrane systematic review highlighted the effectiveness of various therapeutic approaches in addressing psychostimulant misuse, emphasizing the importance of tailored psychosocial strategies. Ashford et al. systematically reviewed digital recovery support services for substance use disorder recovery. Their findings underscored the growing role of digital platforms in providing accessible and effective recovery support for individuals with substance use disorders. Nesvåg and McKay explored the feasibility and impact of digital interventions in supporting recovery from substance use disorders. Their systematic review demonstrated the potential of digital tools to enhance recovery outcomes, particularly when integrated into comprehensive care models. Wasmuth et al. conducted a systematic review on occupation-based interventions for addictive disorders. Their findings suggested that engaging individuals in meaningful occupational activities can play a critical role in addiction recovery and overall well-being. Giménez-Meseguer et al. examined the benefits of physical exercise on mental health and quality of life in patients with substance use disorders. Their systematic review and meta-analysis provided robust evidence supporting the integration of exercise into treatment plans for these individuals. Sancho et al. reviewed mindfulness-based interventions for treating substance and behavioral addictions. Their systematic review highlighted the efficacy of mindfulness practices in reducing addictive behaviors and improving psychological outcomes. Beraldo et al. discussed the role of spirituality and religiosity in addiction recovery. Their review emphasized the therapeutic value of incorporating spiritual and religious elements into recovery programs for individuals with substance use disorders. Walton-Moss et al. systematically reviewed the relationship between spirituality or religion and recovery from substance abuse. Their findings reinforced the positive association between spiritual practices and improved recovery outcomes. Vest et al. conducted a PRISMA-guided scoping review on college programming for students in addiction recovery. Their research highlighted the importance of tailored support systems within academic settings to facilitate recovery and academic success. Magura and Marshall updated a systematic review on interventions aimed at improving employment outcomes for individuals with substance use disorders. Their findings emphasized the critical role of employment-focused programs in supporting long-term recovery. Harrison et al. reviewed individual placement and support (IPS) employment interventions for individuals with substance use disorders. Their systematic review demonstrated the effectiveness of IPS in enhancing employment outcomes and recovery trajectories. Akanbi et al. systematically reviewed employer-led interventions for addressing drug misuse. Their findings highlighted the potential of workplace-based programs to reduce substance misuse and improve employee well-being. Vanderplasschen et al. conducted a meta-analysis on the efficacy of case management for substance use disorders. Their research provided evidence supporting the role of case management in promoting recovery and improving treatment outcomes. Eddie et al. systematically reviewed peer recovery support services and recovery coaching for substance use disorders. Their findings underscored the value of lived experience in enhancing recovery outcomes and fostering community support. Reif et al. assessed the evidence for peer recovery support for individuals with substance use disorders. Their review highlighted the effectiveness of peer-led interventions in improving recovery outcomes and reducing relapse rates. Tracy and Wallace reviewed the benefits of peer support groups in addiction treatment. Their findings emphasized the importance of peer networks in fostering a sense of belonging and accountability during recovery. Gormley et al. systematically reviewed the effectiveness of peer recovery support services across the opioid use disorder treatment cascade. Their research demonstrated the positive impact of peer support on treatment engagement and retention. Orock and Nicette reviewed the literature on peer-based recovery support in substance abuse treatment, with implications for implementation in Seychelles. Their findings highlighted the adaptability and effectiveness of peer support models in diverse cultural contexts. Bassuk et al. systematically reviewed peer-delivered recovery support services for addictions in the United States. Their research provided evidence for the scalability and efficacy of peer-led interventions in addiction recovery. Beck et al. systematically reviewed SMART Recovery programs, focusing on outcomes, process variables, and research implications. Their findings highlighted the structured and evidence-based nature of SMART Recovery in supporting individuals with substance use disorders. De Andrade et al. reviewed the effectiveness of residential treatment services for individuals with substance use disorders. Their systematic review emphasized the importance of structured residential care in achieving sustained recovery. Penzesntadler et al. systematically reviewed the impact of assertive community treatment (ACT) for patients with substance use disorders. Their findings supported the integration of ACT into treatment plans to enhance recovery outcomes. Beaulieu et al. conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on the long-term treatment and support of substance use disorders. Their research highlighted the importance of sustained care in achieving long-term recovery. Austin et al. systematically reviewed the associations between housing stress and later substance use outcomes. Their findings underscored the critical role of stable housing in supporting recovery and preventing relapse. Reif et al. assessed the evidence for recovery housing as a supportive intervention for individuals with substance use disorders. Their review highlighted the benefits of recovery housing in fostering a stable and supportive environment for recovery. Du Plessis et al. systematically reviewed the role of peer support workers in substance abuse treatment services. Their findings emphasized the value of peer support in enhancing treatment engagement and outcomes. Nevitt et al. conducted a network meta-analysis on antiepileptic drug monotherapy for epilepsy, analyzing individual participant data. Their findings provided insights into the comparative efficacy and safety of various antiepileptic drugs. Veroniki et al. systematically reviewed the safety of antiepileptic drugs during pregnancy, focusing on congenital malformations and prenatal outcomes. Their research highlighted the importance of informed decision-making in managing epilepsy during pregnancy. Maguire et al. reviewed treatments for preventing sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). Their findings emphasized the need for targeted interventions to reduce SUDEP risk in individuals with epilepsy. Sveinsson et al. conducted a nationwide population-based cohort study on the incidence of SUDEP. Their research provided valuable epidemiological insights into the prevalence and risk factors associated with SUDEP. Kløvgaard et al. updated the evidence on sudden unexpected death in epilepsy, highlighting advancements in understanding and prevention strategies. Langan et al. conducted a case-control study on SUDEP, providing critical insights into the risk factors and potential preventive measures for this condition. Cheng and Zhang conducted a comprehensive meta-review of nonpharmacological interventions for informal dementia caregivers. Their findings highlighted the importance of supportive interventions in reducing caregiver burden and improving quality of life. Ceraso et al. systematically reviewed maintenance treatment with antipsychotic drugs for schizophrenia. Their findings emphasized the role of long-term antipsychotic therapy in preventing relapse and maintaining symptom control. Leucht et al. conducted a Bayesian meta-analysis of placebo-controlled antipsychotic drug trials in acute schizophrenia. Their research provided insights into the efficacy predictors of antipsychotic medications. Schneider-Thoma et al. systematically reviewed the short-term mortality associated with second-generation antipsychotic drugs. Their findings highlighted the safety profile of these medications in clinical practice. Kishi et al. conducted a meta-analysis on the effects of discontinuation versus maintenance of antipsychotic medication in first-episode psychosis. Their findings emphasized the risks of relapse associated with medication discontinuation. Kishi et al. systematically reviewed recurrence rates in stable bipolar disorder patients after drug discontinuation versus maintenance. Their findings highlighted the importance of continued pharmacological treatment in preventing relapse. Kishi et al. reviewed the efficacy of mood stabilizers and antipsychotics in the maintenance phase of bipolar disorder. Their findings provided evidence for the comparative effectiveness of these treatments in preventing mood episodes. Kishimoto et al. systematically reviewed long-acting injectable versus oral antipsychotics for schizophrenia maintenance treatment. Their findings highlighted the advantages of long-acting injectables in improving adherence and reducing relapse rates. Schneider-Thoma et al. compared the efficacy and tolerability of oral and long-acting injectable antipsychotics for schizophrenia maintenance. Their findings provided evidence for the individualized selection of antipsychotic formulations. Krause et al. conducted a network meta-analysis on the efficacy and tolerability of antipsychotics in children and adolescents with schizophrenia. Their findings emphasized the importance of age-appropriate treatment strategies. Del Bello et al. systematically reviewed second-generation antipsychotics for bipolar depression in youth. Their findings highlighted the efficacy and safety of these medications in managing bipolar symptoms in younger populations. Ciray et al. reviewed placebo-controlled pharmacological trials in children and adolescents with bipolar disorder manic episodes. Their findings provided insights into the efficacy and placebo response in this population. Kishi et al. systematically reviewed pharmacological treatments for bipolar mania, focusing on double-blind randomized controlled trials. Their findings highlighted the comparative efficacy of various pharmacological options. Farkas and Feeney reviewed adverse events associated with carbamazepine, providing critical insights into its safety profile. Meador reviewed the effects of in utero antiepileptic drug exposure, emphasizing the importance of monitoring and managing risks during pregnancy. Jochim et al. systematically reviewed the use of valproate for acute mania, providing evidence for its efficacy in managing manic episodes. Yildiz et al. systematically reviewed pharmacological interventions for acute bipolar depression in adults. Their findings highlighted the comparative efficacy and tolerability of available treatments. Bighelli et al. reviewed psychological interventions for reducing positive symptoms in schizophrenia. Their findings emphasized the importance of integrating psychological therapies into treatment plans. Oud et al. systematically reviewed psychological interventions for adults with bipolar disorder. Their findings highlighted the efficacy of these interventions in managing symptoms and preventing relapse. Stallman and Allen reviewed evidence on acute suicide prevention interventions, providing insights into effective clinical practices. Nuij et al. conducted a meta-analysis on safety planning interventions for suicide prevention. Their findings highlighted the efficacy of these interventions in reducing suicide risk. House reviewed safety planning interventions for suicide prevention, emphasizing their role in mitigating suicide risk. Ferguson et al. systematically reviewed the effectiveness of safety planning interventions for adults experiencing suicide-related distress. Their findings highlighted the importance of structured safety planning in clinical practice. Stanley and Brown reviewed the safety planning intervention as a brief strategy to mitigate suicide risk. Their findings emphasized its utility in clinical settings. Till et al. evaluated the impact of a suicide-awareness campaign on the utilization of a telephone emergency line in Austria. Their findings highlighted the importance of public awareness initiatives in suicide prevention. The World Health Organization and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees developed the mhGAP Humanitarian Intervention Guide (mhGAP-HIG) to address mental, neurological, and substance use conditions in humanitarian emergencies. This guide provides evidence-based recommendations for clinical management in resource-limited settings.
